source_text:
This week I did around 40 code reviews. About 8 a day. It sounds impressive until you admit what it actually means: you can’t review at that pace, while still writing code yourself, without drastically lowering the quality of your reviews.
One PR this week made me see it. I don’t review test files anymore. Unit tests, the base of the pyramid, the majority of our tests. I skip them. Not because they don’t matter. Because halfway through a big diff I tell myself, “those are just tests, I have enough files to get through.”
And this is exactly the wrong time to skip them. A lot of AI generated tests are useless. Worse, I forgot that reading the tests is how you actually understand what the code is supposed to do. Skipping them means you’re not really reviewing the PR.
That’s a habit I built without noticing, and it’s a bad one.
So here’s what I’m changing. Test files get reviewed with the same attention as the code they cover. I open them first, like in the good old days, because they tell me what the code claims to do before I read how it does it. And if that means fewer reviews per week, then fewer is the honest number.
Do you skip test files too, or is it just me?
